checks.claim: Two maternity clinics at Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s; doctors and medical students in the First, midwives in the Second
checks.note: Also https://grokipedia.com/page/Ignaz_Semmelweis and the MJA 2018 article.

checks.claim: First Clinic lost about one mother in ten to childbed fever
checks.note: JLL: 98.4 per 1,000 births, 1840-1846; Wikipedia: average about 10%.

checks.claim: Second Clinic lost fewer than one in twenty-five
checks.note: JLL: 36.2 per 1,000 (under 40 per 1,000 = 1 in 25); Wikipedia: averaged less than 4%. True as an average (single years ran higher, e.g. 7.6% in 1842).

checks.claim: Admissions alternated between the clinics, a day at a time
checks.note: Semmelweis 1861 (via JLL): admissions alternated through twenty-four hour periods, First four days a week, Second three. 'Took turns, a day at a time' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Key: the rota ruled out that one clinic was sent the sicker women
checks.note: JLL: 'no clinical selection of cases for either clinic'; the rota produced 'by accident rather than design, a controlled trial'. This is exactly selection bias.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'That the doctors' own work explained the gap' (not ruled out; it was the real cause)
Wrong: 'That foul air in the hospital caused the fever' (allocation says nothing about the air; a miasmatist could still say the First Clinic's air was worse)
checks.note: Miasma was argued against from the shared building and the street births, not from the rota. Not ruled out by the sorting itself.

checks.claim: Wrong: 'That fear of the First Clinic made women ill' (women who dreaded the First Clinic were still sent there by the day; the rota cannot rule out fear)
Context: 'by accident, a controlled trial'; Semmelweis went on to suspect the doctors' own work
Jakob Kolletschka was a professor at Vienna General Hospital
checks.note: Professor of forensic medicine at Vienna General Hospital; Semmelweis's friend.

checks.claim: Pricked by a student's scalpel during an autopsy
checks.note: 'his finger was pricked by a student with the same knife that was being used in the autopsy'; also Grokipedia Ignaz_Semmelweis and MJA 2018.

checks.claim: The prick happened 'in March 1847' and he 'soon died'
checks.note: Sources date only his DEATH, 13 March 1847 (Grokipedia, Wikipedia). No source found dates the injury; his illness ran through lymphangitis, phlebitis, pleurisy, pericarditis, peritonitis, meningitis and an eye metastasis, so the cut may well have been in late February. Fix: 'was pricked by a student's scalpel during an autopsy and died in March 1847.'

checks.claim: His autopsy showed the same signs as mothers dead of childbed fever
checks.note: Grokipedia: suppuration and inflammatory infiltration resembling the women's; Wikipedia: pathology similar.

checks.claim: Key: matter from a corpse, entering a cut, could cause it
checks.note: MJA: his death 'was clearly caused by his inoculation with cadaverous particles from the contaminated knife' (Semmelweis's conclusion).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: foul air in the autopsy room / fear and shock / a chill
checks.note: None is what Semmelweis drew from the death; the cut is the distinguishing fact. Each is a cause in the textbooks of the day (Braun's list), so they are honest lures.

checks.claim: Context: 'cadaverous particles' carried on hands of doctors and students
checks.note: Semmelweis's own term; also MJA, Grokipedia.

checks.claim: Context: bad air, emotional shock and chilling appeared in textbooks as causes
checks.note: Carl Braun's textbook listed 30 causes including emotional trauma, chilling, atmospheric epidemic influences; cadaverous infection 28th.

checks.claim: Context: the student midwives of the safer clinic never touched a corpse
checks.note: MJA: 'doctors and medical students performed autopsies, but midwives did not'. 'Did no autopsies' would be the exact wording; 'never touched a corpse' is a slight stretch but acceptable.

checks.claim: Handwashing in chlorinated lime from May 1847
checks.note: Wikipedia: started mid-May 1847; Grokipedia: May 1847.

checks.claim: Deaths fell from 18.3% in April to 1.2% in July (1847)
checks.note: Grokipedia and Wikipedia agree: April 18.3%, June 2.2%, July 1.2%, August 1.9%.

checks.claim: Johann Klein, head of the clinic, never accepted the idea
checks.note: MJA: 'Even Klein ... never accepted Semmelweis' theory'.

checks.claim: Key: he could not show what the particles were and how they did harm
checks.note: Grokipedia: Klein demanded mechanisms, not just statistical correlation; Scanzoni said the agent had not been isolated. Wikipedia: he offered 'no theoretical explanation'; Levy doubted the unspecified cadaverous particles. The accepted reading.

checks.claim: Wrong: he could not show how his clinic's deaths ran in the years before
checks.note: He had the yearly figures (Wikipedia's 1841-1846 table).

checks.claim: Wrong: he could not show how the midwives' clinic compared / how many women each took in
checks.note: His tables give births and deaths for both clinics.

checks.claim: Context: the fall held through 1848
checks.note: 1848 annual rate 1.27% (Grokipedia); 1.3% (MJA).

checks.claim: Context: no one could yet see or name what was being carried; Klein wanted more than statistics; germ theory explained it after his death
checks.note: No agent had been identified (germ theory came in the 1860s-1870s). Acceptable.

checks.claim: Context: died in an asylum near Vienna in 1865, aged 47, of an infected wound on his hand
checks.note: Year, age 47 and the infected (gangrenous) wound on his right hand, with pyaemia, are right (Wikipedia, Grokipedia, MJA). But 'near Vienna' follows Grokipedia's Doebling account; Wikipedia's text and Wilkinson (Br J Psychiatry 2021) say Hebra took him to the public Lower Austrian asylum in the Lazarettgasse, beside the General Hospital, in Vienna itself. Sources disagree. Fix: 'he died in an asylum in Vienna in 1865' (true on either account, since Doebling is now part of Vienna).

checks.claim: John Snow, London doctor; cholera killed hundreds in Soho in 1854; he blamed the Broad Street pump's water, most doctors blamed bad air
checks.note: Also Wikipedia 1854_Broad_Street_cholera_outbreak (miasma dominant; General Board of Health blamed miasma).

checks.claim: Key: brewery men by the pump, who drank only beer, dying as often as others would have counted most against him
checks.note: Correct reasoning: men exposed to the street's air but not the pump's water are the test case for miasma vs water. Snow 1855: the men had a malt-liquor allowance and Mr Huggins 'believes they do not drink water at all' and was 'quite certain' they never used the street pump (the brewery also had its own deep well). 'Drank only beer' is the owner's belief, fair at this level; 'who never drank from the pump' would be safer.

checks.claim: Wrong: families who walked past nearer pumps to fetch its water falling ill (supports Snow; he really found it)
checks.note: Snow: five families 'always sent to the pump in Broad Street, as they preferred the water to that of the pumps which were nearer'.

checks.claim: Wrong: deaths crowding closest to the pump (supports Snow; he really found it)
checks.note: Clustering fits water (and could fit a local miasma), but cannot count AGAINST him.

checks.claim: Wrong: a widow miles away, sent its water by cart, dying of cholera (supports Snow; he really found it)
checks.note: Snow 1855: widow at West End, Hampstead, aged 59 (register); a cart went from Broad Street to West End daily with a large bottle of the pump water; she died on Saturday 2 September; no cholera at West End then. Hampstead is a few miles from Soho.

checks.claim: Context: none of the brewery's seventy-odd workmen fell seriously ill
checks.note: Snow 1855: 'above seventy workmen', none had suffered from cholera, 'at least in a severe form', only two indisposed and not seriously. NB Grokipedia is wrong here: its John Snow page gives the brewery 'over 500 employees, 5 deaths' and its outbreak page 18 employees; the 535 inmates with 5 deaths were the Poland Street workhouse. The draft rightly uses Snow's own figure.

checks.claim: Context: a test that could have proved him wrong and did not made his case stronger
Snow persuaded the parish; handle removed 8 September 1854
checks.note: Snow: interview with the Board of Guardians of St James's parish on the evening of Thursday 7 September; 'the handle of the pump was removed on the following day'. Grokipedia agrees on 8 September (it says the Vestry).

checks.claim: Many retellings end with the handle as the proof (popular myth)
checks.note: Wikipedia and Grokipedia both note the epidemic was already declining; the stem tells the popular version as overclaim, correctly.

checks.claim: Snow wrote the removal could not settle whether the well still held the poison
checks.note: Snow: attacks 'had so far diminished before the use of the water was stopped, that it is impossible to decide whether the well still contained the cholera poison in an active state'.

checks.claim: Key: deaths had already been falling for days before it
checks.note: Grokipedia: already on a downward trajectory, peak passed; Whitehead: 'steadily on the decline for several days before the pump-handle was removed'.

checks.claim: Wrong: every other pump in Soho shut that day
checks.note: No source; only the Broad Street handle was removed.

checks.claim: Wrong: the handle was put back within a few days
checks.note: Officials replaced it only 'after the cholera epidemic subsided'; in any case not Snow's reason.

checks.claim: Wrong: most of the dead had never drunk from that pump
checks.note: Contrary to Snow's findings.

checks.claim: Context: fatal attacks 143 on 1 September, 12 on 8 September
checks.note: Snow's Table 1: 143 and 12 (Whitehead's table gave 142 and 14).

checks.claim: Context: partly because many people had fled
checks.note: Snow: 'the mortality was much diminished ... by the flight of the population'; Wikipedia: three quarters of residents fled within a week.

checks.claim: Felix Pouchet, Pasteur's rival, defended spontaneous generation (life from lifeless matter)
checks.note: Public dispute 1859-1864 (Wikipedia Swan_neck_flask).

checks.claim: Pouchet held that life needs the oxygen in air to arise
checks.note: Wikipedia: the flask 'answered Pouchet's claim that the oxygen in air was needed for life to arise'. Pouchet held putrescible matter, air and water to be the necessary conditions (Encyclopedia.com / Wikipedia Pouchet); his 1858 note reported life arising in artificial air and in oxygen gas.

checks.claim: S-shaped neck drawn out, open at the tip; broth boiled
Key: air could reach the broth, but dust stuck in the bend
checks.note: Air moves in and out; particles 'settle or adhere to the moist glass of the bend'. Grokipedia and OpenStax agree.

checks.claim: Wrong: air reached the broth only once heated
checks.note: The point of the design was untreated air (contrast Schwann's heated air).

checks.claim: Wrong: the bend kept the air off the broth while it cooled
checks.note: The classic misconception; air moved freely.

checks.claim: Wrong: air could reach the broth, but its oxygen could not
checks.note: Physically false; the neck is open.

checks.claim: Context: Schwann had earlier fed broth heated air, leaving room to say the heat had changed it
checks.note: Schwann 1837: boiled infusions kept with air 'that had been heated or otherwise treated'.

checks.claim: Context: life in spoiled broth comes from specks carried in the air, not the air itself
checks.note: Pasteur concluded airborne particles, not the air or a 'vital force', carried the organisms.

checks.claim: Swan-necked flask stayed clear; neck snapped off near the body; broth soon cloudy
checks.note: Breaking the neck near the flask body let air touch the liquid directly and 'the broth quickly turned cloudy'. Grokipedia: broke the neck tips, rapid proliferation.

checks.claim: Key: the boil had not ruined the broth as food for microbes
checks.note: Answers the objection that 'Pasteur's prolonged heating had destroyed the broth's capacity to support life' (Wikipedia attributes it to Pouchet; it is also Needham's old 'vegetative force' objection, Grokipedia). The accepted reading of the step.

checks.claim: Wrong: lifeless dust can turn into living microbes
checks.note: Pasteur's conclusion: the particles carry living organisms.

checks.claim: Wrong: a few microbes had lived through the boil all along
checks.note: Survivors would have clouded the intact flask; it stayed clear until the neck was broken.

checks.claim: Wrong: the bend had been keeping the air out
checks.note: Air passed freely; only particles were caught.

checks.claim: Context: tipping an unbroken flask so the broth washed the bend clouded it too
checks.note: Same result when an intact flask was tilted so the liquid reached the neck where particles had settled; Grokipedia also reports tilting.

checks.claim: Koch was a country doctor (district medical officer) in Wollstein; 1870s; set out to prove the anthrax rod was the cause
checks.note: Grokipedia: district medical officer in Wollstein, Prussia; anthrax work published 1876 via Cohn. Nobel biography (nobelprize.org, quoted in search): he 'set himself to prove scientifically that this bacillus is, in fact, the cause'.

checks.claim: Home-made slivers of wood; rods from spleens of animals dead of anthrax into mice; all died; at the same time mice given healthy spleen blood
checks.note: Nobel biography: inoculated mice 'by means of home-made slivers of wood' with bacilli from spleens of farm animals dead of anthrax; 'all killed', whereas mice inoculated at the same time with blood from spleens of healthy animals did not suffer from the disease.

checks.claim: Key: the control ruled out that the cut or any spleen blood could kill a mouse
checks.note: A control has identical conditions except the tested variable; same wound and same kind of material, minus the sick animal's contents.

checks.claim: Wrong: that something else in the sick blood did the killing (not ruled out)
checks.note: Exactly why Koch went on to pure cultures with no animal contact.

checks.claim: Wrong: rods grow only in a living body / spread through the air of a farm
checks.note: Neither is addressed by the control; the first is in fact false (he grew them outside the body).

checks.claim: Context: grew the rods several generations in fluid from an ox's eye, far from any animal, and they still caused anthrax
checks.note: Nobel biography: grew the bacilli for several generations in pure cultures, and 'although they had had no contact with any kind of animal, they could still cause anthrax'; culture medium the aqueous humour (cattle/ox eye) per Nobel biography and Encyclopedia.com.

checks.claim: 'Robert Koch laid down four steps, known as Koch's postulates'
checks.note: Wikipedia: formulated by Koch and Loeffler in 1884 (on Henle's ideas), refined by Koch in 1890, and 'The fourth postulate was added later'; Loeffler's 1884 statement had three steps (Gradmann; Heidelberg abstract). Grokipedia, by contrast, says 'The four postulates, as stated by Koch'. The four-step list is the textbook form, not strictly Koch's own. Fix: 'Koch's postulates, the steps named after Robert Koch for proving that a particular germ causes a particular disease, are now taught as four.' The question itself does not hinge on step 4.

checks.claim: Working on cholera, he later found its germ in people with no sign of disease
checks.note: Koch found asymptomatic carriers of cholera and later typhoid (Wikipedia); Grokipedia: most cholera infections mild or asymptomatic, pathogen isolable from healthy shedders, against the first postulate.

checks.claim: Key: the step given up in part was 'found in all the sick and in none of the well'
checks.note: 'Koch later abandoned the universalist requirement of the first postulate altogether when he discovered asymptomatic carriers'.

checks.claim: Wrong: grown pure, apart from the body
checks.note: Carriers do not touch this step (viruses do).

checks.claim: Wrong: 'The pure germ should bring on the disease in a healthy animal'
checks.note: Not given up: the step already says 'should', not 'must', because not everyone exposed falls ill. A sharp student could link carriers to this step, but the documented step Koch gave up is the first; the 'should' already in this choice marks it as the hedged one. Acceptable.

checks.claim: Wrong: the germ is found again in the animal that fell ill
Context: most people infected with cholera have mild symptoms or none
checks.note: WHO: 'Most people infected with V. cholerae do not develop symptoms'; most with the disease have mild or moderate symptoms.

checks.claim: Context: viruses cannot be grown pure outside living cells
checks.note: Obligate intracellular parasites; violate the second postulate.

checks.claim: Joseph Lister, surgeon in Glasgow
checks.note: Regius Professor of Surgery, Glasgow, 1860; surgeon to the Glasgow Royal Infirmary 1861.

checks.claim: Nearly half of his amputation patients died
checks.note: Lister 1870: 16 deaths in 35 cases (about 45%) before antisepsis; Grokipedia about 46% for 1864-1866.

checks.claim: Surgeons blamed the rot on the oxygen in the air
checks.note: Lister 1867: oxygen 'universally regarded as the agent by which putrefaction was effected'. (Grokipedia adds that bad-air miasma views were also held; the stem's claim is Lister's own.)

checks.claim: After reading Pasteur's work, Lister tried a new plan in 1865
checks.note: Read Pasteur on fermentation and putrefaction in 1865; first carbolic dressing on James Greenlees, 12 August 1865.

checks.claim: Key: destroy the living specks that reached each wound
checks.note: Lister: a dressing 'capable of destroying the life of the floating particles'.

checks.claim: Wrong: seal each wound so no oxygen could reach it
checks.note: Lister: 'it seemed hopeless to attempt to exclude the oxygen'; his insight was that he need not.

checks.claim: Wrong: clear the wards of foul vapours / amputate sooner
checks.note: Miasma-era measures, not Lister's plan.

checks.claim: Context: carbolic acid, then used on the sewage of Carlisle
checks.note: Lister 1867: 'much struck with an account of the remarkable effects produced by carbolic acid upon the sewage of the town of Carlisle'; Grokipedia: Calvert's Carlisle work, reported in The Times 1864.

checks.claim: Context: amputation deaths fell from 16 of 35 to 6 of 40
checks.note: Lister's own 1870 figures; he called them 'too small for a satisfactory statistical comparison'.

checks.claim: Context: critics asked whether other changes explained the fall; The Lancet urged a side-by-side ward test
checks.note: JLL: The Lancet urged 'again and again' that 'one ward should be set aside ... where antisepsis might be exclusively used and a comparison made'; critics noted improved hygiene and technique; Grokipedia: critics questioned whether the method caused the fall.

unit_notes: 7 ok, 0 error, 3 uncertain (all small wording fixes). Grokipedia errors confirmed against Snow 1855 (UCLA epi-snow): (1) Grokipedia's John Snow page says Lambeth customers died at 8-9 times the Southwark and Vauxhall rate; Snow's Table IX gives the reverse, 315 deaths per 10,000 houses for Southwark and Vauxhall against 37 for Lambeth. (2) Grokipedia gives the Broad Street brewery 'over 500 employees, 5 deaths' or 18 employees; Snow: 'above seventy workmen', none with severe cholera (the 535 inmates and 5 deaths were the Poland Street workhouse). Neither error reached the draft. The Semmelweis asylum: Grokipedia and Deutsche Biographie say Doebling, near Vienna; Wikipedia's text and Wilkinson (Br J Psychiatry 2021) say the public asylum in the Lazarettgasse, Vienna; avoid 'near Vienna'. The admission rota (24-hour turns, First Clinic four days a week, Second three) is confirmed only by Semmelweis 1861 via the James Lind Library; Grokipedia and Wikipedia do not describe it.
